“The Innovator's Dilemma”  by Clayton M. Christensen described how big companies fail when against new startups because they can’t let go of their fat margins for a new technology that (at first) appears to be inferior, even a toy. (His examples are Japanese motorbikes and hard disks) 

Seems the United States is now trapped in the same dilemma. It can’t let go of those fat oil profits to embrace the new —but rapidly improving— renewable tech, even if it’s clear that that’s where the market for energy is heading. I.E., the big company (or nation) must sabotage some of their current profit centers in order to remain long term competitive.

I reported this story when I was in China for President Trump's visit in May. I took a side trip to southeastern China to visit the world's largest cluster of battery factories, and what I saw was incredibly impressive -- the world's most advanced battery technology, funded by years of intensive research. The tech is critical to cars in China — about half of the cars on the road in major Chinese cities seemed to be EVs now - but also buses and trucks, as well as data centers and renewable power generation more broadly. 

China’s achievements in this and other areas flip the script on past decades in the US China relationship, where traditionally US companies had the advanced technology. The achievements also pose a tough challenge for US officials. Major auto companies like Tesla and Ford are already partnering with CATL. 

The tech can go a long way to spreading EV adoption and reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and rivals don’t have anything like it. But we are coming off a year where China weaponized its control over a supply chain — that for rare earth minerals. So the question for US official is where the United States should depend on Chinese suppliers, and where it shouldn't. 

As a reporter I really like writing stories that elucidate both sides of an argument but then let readers decide for themselves. Let me know what you think about this debate and if I left anything out.

“The Innovator's Dilemma” by Clayton M. Christensen described how big companies fail when against new startups because they can’t let go of their fat margins for a new technology that (at first) appears to be inferior, even a toy. (His examples are Japanese motorbikes and hard disks)

Seems the United States is now trapped in the same dilemma. It can’t let go of those fat oil profits to embrace the new —but rapidly improving— renewable tech, even if it’s clear that that’s where the market for energy is heading. I.E., the big company (or nation) must sabotage some of their current profit centers in order to remain long term competitive.

“The Innovator's Dilemma”  by Clayton M. Christensen described how big companies fail when against new startups because they can’t let go of their fat margins for a new technology that (at first) appears to be inferior, even a toy. (His examples are Japanese motorbikes and hard disks) 

Seems the United States is now trapped in the same dilemma. It can’t let go of those fat oil profits to embrace the new —but rapidly improving— renewable tech, even if it’s clear that that’s where the market for energy is heading. I.E., the big company (or nation) must sabotage some of their current profit centers in order to remain long term competitive.

Watch YouTube videos on China's new EVs, or the top 10 EVs in China. It's mind-blowing.  Ford's CEO said that visiting China and driving Chinese EVs was the most humbling experience of his life.  There are Chinese cars that can swim in floods and rivers; have small fridges and safes; in-car movie screens (back seat), endless sensors, can rotate 360º in place like a battle tank, etc.  Incredible.

China has 100,000 engineers in its auto industry.  They are making remarkable progress in battery life, safety, charge-time and cold-weather performance. One supposed limitation after another is falling to R&D.

The US gas-engine automakers are doomed to shrinkage and irrelevance. They are the Blockbuster video when Netflix arrived; the BlackBerry when iPhone arrived. “The Innovator's Dilemma”  by Clayton M. Christensen described how big companies fail when against new startups because they can’t let go of their fat margins for a new technology that (at first) appears to be inferior, even a toy. (His examples are Japanese motorbikes and hard disks) 

Seems the United States is now trapped in the same dilemma. It can’t let go of those fat oil profits to embrace the new —but rapidly improving— renewable tech, even if it’s clear that that’s where the market for energy is heading. I.E., the big company (or nation) must sabotage some of their current profit centers in order to remain long term competitive.

One reads this and sees decades of American foolishness and greed leading to our fall from top tier research and manufacturing. We innovate and invent but rather than make it here, to enhance profits, companies move the manufacturing to inexpensive China. China demands technological sharing in these joint ventures, then takes the knowledge to develop their own independent battery industry that dominates the world. Now as icing on the cake, we have an aggressively ignorant administration eager to please fossil fuel billionaires destroying all progress and government support for EVs as well as gutting research in numerous areas. Time is very short for good leadership and bipartisan support to reverse this decline.

This should be framed as support for engineering work as opposed to new scientific breakthroughs. The chemistries which are being tried are relatively known and expanding into them is not leading into scientific breakthroughs but engineering progress. A semantic point, but it should help frame this conversation. China's dominance in this field is through the massive support their government has given, as well as the technology transfers through companies....and yes...non-chinese universities. It has really worked. The US, in my opinion, should not castigate China for this but use it as a model to do the same thing. Subsidies are needed and some protectionism is needed no to support US based companies. My hope is that enough is done to provide much more environmentally friendly mining operations. That will be quite expensive but if allowed to grow can become a new standard around the world. Let us not be blind to what China has done but respond constructively to it.

"U.S. firms came to China to manufacture their goods more cheaply. As a price of entry, the Chinese government forced foreign companies into partnerships where Chinese firms could learn from them and absorb their more advanced technology."

In other words, US CEOs and investors CHOSE to manufacture in China and give up control of their technological developments.  Then later they came begging (demanding?) that states, localities, and the federal government give them tax breaks.

And those corporations kept insisting that they were innocent dupes who lost IP to the sneaky Chinese companies and government.  Unfortunately, the public mostly bought that quarter-truth.

Another loss was the loss of impetus for students to go into engineering, science, and the like in favor of careers in banking/finance/investment.  Suggestions that the US develop a manufacturing plan and invest in high skill job education and training were mostly ignored, especially if advocated by unions.

As Democrats, we should say clearly: Joe Biden was right and Donald Trump is wrong. Biden understood that the future of the auto industry is electric, software-driven, and globally competitive — and that America needed to invest, innovate, and lead. Trump’s rollback of clean air standards and embrace of fossil fuels may juice short-term pickup profits, but it leaves us strategically weaker while China races ahead.

Companies like BYD shouldn’t be feared — they should be challenged in an open market that forces American automakers to compete and improve. The U.S. pioneered modern EV technology and advanced battery research. What held us back wasn’t lack of ingenuity; it was corporate complacency, political hubris, and decades of pressure from the oil and gas lobby telling Americans the future was always one more pipeline away.

If General Motors and Ford Motor Company become relics, it won’t be because China cheated — it will be because we chose protection over progress. America doesn’t win by hiding from competition. We win by building better technology, investing in workers, and leading the clean energy transition instead of pretending it isn’t happening.

Watch YouTube videos on China's new EVs, or the top 10 EVs in China. It's mind-blowing.  Ford's CEO said that visiting China and driving Chinese EVs was the most humbling experience of his life.  There are Chinese cars that can swim in floods and rivers; have small fridges and safes; in-car movie screens (back seat), endless sensors, can rotate 360º in place like a battle tank, etc.  Incredible.

China has 100,000 engineers in its auto industry.  They are making remarkable progress in battery life, safety, charge-time and cold-weather performance. One supposed limitation after another is falling to R&D.

The US gas-engine automakers are doomed to shrinkage and irrelevance. They are the Blockbuster video when Netflix arrived; the BlackBerry when iPhone arrived.  They mastered a technology (combustion engines) that is now obsolete except for niche applications.  Chinese OEMs deliver astonishing value for the price, and their tech is way ahead of America's car industry in everything from suspension to in-car electronics and use of sensors.  The factories are super-modern, with intensive use of robots for efficiency, precision and finish.

If America allowed Chinese EVs into its market, there would be lines of people at the dealers, like when iPhones came out and people lined up at Apple stores.  What you get for the price is amazing, and the build-quality is superb.  People who own them love them.

I reported this story when I was in China for President Trump's visit in May. I took a side trip to southeastern China to visit the world's largest cluster of battery factories, and what I saw was incredibly impressive -- the world's most advanced battery technology, funded by years of intensive research. The tech is critical to cars in China — about half of the cars on the road in major Chinese cities seemed to be EVs now - but also buses and trucks, as well as data centers and renewable power generation more broadly.

China’s achievements in this and other areas flip the script on past decades in the US China relationship, where traditionally US companies had the advanced technology. The achievements also pose a tough challenge for US officials. Major auto companies like Tesla and Ford are already partnering with CATL.

The tech can go a long way to spreading EV adoption and reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and rivals don’t have anything like it. But we are coming off a year where China weaponized its control over a supply chain — that for rare earth minerals. So the question for US official is where the United States should depend on Chinese suppliers, and where it shouldn't.

As a reporter I really like writing stories that elucidate both sides of an argument but then let readers decide for themselves. Let me know what you think about this debate and if I left anything out.
